                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.

=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

- P-84 **Storage is `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes.** A high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. - P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with array decisions A, B and D (PLAN item 13).** The three: a store per element type chosen by the factory, the size also kept as a field of the store, and a factory for a size known only at run time that returns the unsized `Array`. A is how `double[]` goes under a float vector, B where unboxed arithmetic happens, D sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is done before the switch-over. **The class loader.** It complicates the "type name" answer a little, not a lot. A generic object on the compiled path is a class stamped by the loader at run time, with the type arguments spliced into the class name under the runtime's own naming convention. So the Java class name of a `Just[\ZZ32\]` is a mangled string, and printing it raw is what makes the team's line ugly. Two ways to get the Fortress name back, both already half-present: decode the class name with the same naming helper the loader uses to encode it, or ask the object's run-time type descriptor, which every stamped class carries so that type tests work. One detail to settle then is whether a generic instance prints `Just` or `Just[\ZZ32\]`, and the interpreter's answer decides it, since the compiled side copies the interpreter. A few lines either way, not a redesign.

**The hashes.** The `@1b6d3586` in Java, Scala and Kotlin is the object's identity hash in hexadecimal. The JVM assigns each object an arbitrary number when first asked for it. It is stable for that object's life, says nothing about its contents, and differs from run to run. Its only job is to tell two instances apart in debug output. For Fortress it would be a poor fit: a `value object` like `Nothing` has no identity to hash, and any run-to-run variation in printed output breaks the differential check between the two paths.

So the shape stays: the Fortress type name on both paths, with or without a bracket marker, no hash.

1:# Judgement: what an object with no `asString` of its own should print
9:## 1. The ground
54:## 2. Alternatives
68:## 3. Interop: should a Java caller's `toString()` equal `asString`?
79:## 4. Other languages, weighed for Fortress
91:## 5. Recommendation
## 5. Recommendation

Adopt the interpreter's convention on both paths: the bare Fortress type name, static arguments in `[\ \]`,
nothing else (B). Implement it as one new native in `nativeHelpers/stringOps.java` that derives the name from
`getClass().getName()` by the steps in section 1, imported at `CompilerBuiltin.fss:282` and used as the
`Object.asString` default at `:350`; leave `FValue.toString` alone, so a Java or Scala caller sees exactly what
`println` shows. Same native, two lines more: give the compiled `Object` a `getter ilkName()` and restore the
interpreter's five-line article `asDebugString` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:43-48`) in place of `:352`, so the debug
rendering agrees too. Reasons in plain words: it is the only alternative under which the three cases print the
same text on both paths without touching the interpreter or its 382 green tests; it makes singletons print
their names; it fixes all three entry points (print, throw, transactions) because all go through `asString`;
it costs about twenty lines in one file plus two one-line library edits; and it leaves the interop rule
`toString = asString` intact. If a marker is still wanted, put it in `asDebugString` on both paths rather than
in `asString`; if it must be in `asString`, D2 is the only sound form, and its price is re-baselining the
interpreter tests, which should be counted before choosing it.

**Default (accept without reading the argument):** *bare type name, walk's spelling, both paths* --
`Box`, `Box[\ZZ32\]`, `Pt`; no marker, no identity hash; a new `stringOps` native behind `Object.asString` at
`CompilerBuiltin.fss:350`; `FValue.toString` unchanged; tuple/arrow argument spelling checked by one probe when
the helper is written.

Resume exists, but it works at the granularity of finished agents, not of a worker's progress inside its conversation.

What `resumeFromRunId` replays is the run's journal: for every `agent()` call whose result was recorded, the script gets that result back instantly and skips the call; the first call without a recorded result, and everything after it, runs live from its prompt. The journal of the dead run has three lines: `launched`, `started rung:R1`, `started rung:R2`. No agent had finished, so nothing was cached, and a resume would have started both workers from their prompts exactly as a relaunch does. The harness does not replay a subagent's own half-finished transcript; that transcript is on disk, but only as a record.

Two consequences:

- The advantage you remember is real one level up. Had the restart come during the skeptics, a resume would have handed the script both rung results at once and re-run only the skeptics. Inside the scatter, with two long-running workers, there was nothing to replay.
- Below agent granularity, the state carrier is git, not the harness. That is what the wip branches did here: the relaunched workers found their tests and R1's fix on their branches and were told to continue from them. The script edit would have invalidated the cache anyway, since the cache key is a hash of the prompt and options, and the prefix changed.
